subject: Critical Thinking
title: Philip Tetlock: Superforecasters and the Science of Prediction
description: A short lesson to help you apply Philip Tetlock: Superforecasters and the Science of Prediction.

hook.text: Expert political predictions are barely better than chance – often worse than a dart-throwing chimp.

buildup.text: Tetlock tracked 28,000 predictions by 284 experts over 20 years.

discovery.text: But some people – 'superforecasters' – were remarkably accurate. What did they have? Not expertise.

twist.text: Foxes beat hedgehogs. The worst predictors were the most famous – because media rewards confidence, not accuracy.

climax.text: Superforecaster traits: they think in probabilities, update with new evidence, seek disconfirming information, & say.

punchline.text: The best forecasters stay humble, update often, and treat belief as probability.

quiz.question: What traits do Tetlock's 'superforecasters' share?
options: Intellectual humility, probabilistic thinking, and constant updating with new evidence

details.summary: Philip Tetlock's research showed that most expert predictions are barely better than chance, but a select group of 'superforecasters' consistently outperform. Their secret is not intelligence but method: they think probabilistically and update constantly.
details.whyItMatters: Tetlock proved that prediction accuracy is a learnable skill, and his research identified specific habits that anyone can adopt to improve their forecasting.
takeaways: Most expert predictions are not much better than random guessing
Superforecasters use probabilistic thinking and frequent updating
Foxes (who know many things) outperform hedgehogs (who know one big thing)

faq.question: What distinguishes superforecasters from average forecasters?
faq.answer: They assign numerical probabilities rather than vague words, they update frequently as new information arrives, they break complex questions into sub-questions, and they track their accuracy honestly. Humility and method beat confidence and intuition.

faq.question: What is the fox-hedgehog distinction in Tetlock's research?
faq.answer: Hedgehogs interpret the world through one big idea and make confident predictions. Foxes draw on many frameworks and are more tentative. Tetlock found that foxes consistently make better predictions because they are more flexible and self-correcting.
